passage:
The parent-teacher meeting ran late, and Mohit sir was on his fourteenth family when Divyansh's father sat down, Divyansh standing stiffly behind him.
The mid-term report lay open: 41 in science.
'His cousin Saurabh got 92,' the father said, before Mohit sir could speak. 'Same school, same books. Our neighbour's son also. Only this one is like this.'
Divyansh stared at a crack in the classroom floor. His ears had gone red.
Mohit sir answered the father's questions politely. When the father stepped out to take a phone call, the teacher turned to Divyansh and said quietly, 'One result is a result. It isn't you. I've seen your lab work.'
Divyansh looked up, startled.
'Come to the staff room on Monday, after lunch. We'll look at what went wrong in the paper and make a plan for three weeks. Just us.'
Divyansh nodded once.

qa.q: What mark did Divyansh get in science?
qa.a: Divyansh got 41 in science on the mid-term report.

qa.q: What do Divyansh's red ears and staring at the floor suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he felt ashamed and small while his father compared him with his cousin and the neighbour's son.

qa.q: Why was Mohit sir's quiet word, with a plan for Monday, helpful here?
qa.a: It separated Divyansh from one bad mark and gave him a concrete next step, which comparison could never do.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's father see the result differently if he heard what Mohit sir said?
qa.a: He might realise his son has real strengths the teacher has seen, and that comparing him with others only makes the shame worse.

grounding: It shows a teacher watching a teen face family comparison after a bad result and offering a quiet word that one result is not the person, plus a plan.

passage:
Dear Wasim,
I didn't get to talk to you properly at Nani's on Sunday, with everyone there, so I'm writing instead.
I saw your face when Khala started on about Faiz's rank and Ruksar's percentage, and then turned to you and said, 'And yours?' I saw you go quiet and push the rice around your plate. I wanted to say something then and I didn't. I'm sorry.
So here it is now: one bad board result is one result. It isn't the whole of you. You're the one who fixed Nana's radio and taught me how to use a spreadsheet. That's still true after a 58 in maths.
If you want, come over on Saturday afternoon. We'll look at what went wrong, together, and plan what you want to do about the supplementary exam. No lectures, promise.
Your Devika didi

qa.q: What did Wasim do at the table when Khala asked about the result?
qa.a: Wasim went quiet and pushed the rice around the plate.

qa.q: Why does Devika say sorry in her letter?
qa.a: She feels guilty that she wanted to speak up at Nani's on Sunday and didn't, while Wasim was being compared.

qa.q: What does Devika offer Wasim as a next step?
qa.a: She invites Wasim on Saturday afternoon to look at what went wrong together and plan for the supplementary exam, with no lectures.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel reading this letter after the lunch at Nani's?
qa.a: Wasim may feel less alone and less judged, knowing at least one person in the family sees Wasim as more than a maths mark.

grounding: It shows an older didi who saw a teen being compared with others after a bad result, offering a quiet word that the result is not the person and help to plan.
